label: Volumes in High Dimension
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 311 through 328 and confronts the strange behaviour of volume as dimension grows. We open with the central paradox: the unit ball, the simplest convex body, has a volume that first rises with dimension and then collapses toward zero, reshaping all high-dimensional intuition.

label: Volume of the Unit Ball
notes: The Gamma-function formula for the unit ball volume is the workhorse of the chapter. Students should notice the numerator is bounded relative to the denominator factorial which grows super-exponentially, so the ratio must eventually vanish. We compute a few values to make the rise then fall concrete.

label: Rise Then Collapse
notes: Here we plot the volume sequence so the non-monotone shape is unmistakable. The peak near dimension five surprises everyone the first time. Emphasize that the body still contains the same inscribed structure, yet its total measure shrinks faster than any geometric series once dimension passes the maximum.

label: Cube versus Inscribed Ball
notes: The unit cube keeps its volume in every dimension while its inscribed ball withers away. We contrast the two side by side. The lesson is that the corners of the cube hold essentially all of its mass, and the inscribed ball touches a vanishing fraction as dimension climbs.

label: Mass Near the Boundary
notes: Scaling a convex body by a factor slightly below one removes almost all of its volume in high dimension. We derive the one minus epsilon to the n estimate and interpret it: nearly every point of a high-dimensional body lies in a thin shell hugging the boundary.

label: Mass Near the Equator
notes: For the sphere, almost all surface area sits in a narrow band around any chosen equator. We sketch the Gaussian-width estimate of the cap measure. This concentration of measure means a random direction is nearly orthogonal to any fixed vector, the engine behind dimension reduction.

label: Circumscribed versus Inscribed
notes: Sandwiching a body between an inscribed and a circumscribed ball gives volume bounds, but in high dimension the gap between the two balls is enormous. We make the radius ratio explicit for the cube and show why crude sandwiching loses an exponential factor, motivating better ellipsoids.

label: John's Ellipsoid
notes: John's theorem provides the optimal ellipsoid inside a convex body, tight up to a factor of the dimension for general bodies and only the square root of the dimension for symmetric ones. We state the containment chain and explain it is the best affine-invariant approximation guaranteed.

label: Epsilon-Nets and Covering
notes: A volumetric counting argument bounds the size of an epsilon-net on the sphere or inside a body. We derive the covering number estimate from the ratio of inflated to original volume. This bound is the combinatorial bridge that turns continuous volume facts into finite, checkable statements.

label: Hardness of Volume
notes: Computing the volume of a polytope given by inequalities is hard: exact volume is sharp-P-hard, and deterministic approximation cannot beat an exponential factor. We outline why this happens, contrasting it with the randomized polynomial-time approximation scheme that uses random walks to sample the body.

label: Large-Volume Polytopes
notes: Few facets cannot capture most of the ball's volume. We sketch the lower bound showing that any polytope approximating the ball to within a constant factor needs exponentially many facets in the dimension. This is the polytope-approximation companion to the covering bound and explains why simple descriptions fail.

label: Isoperimetry in High Dimension
notes: The isoperimetric inequality says the ball minimizes surface area for a fixed volume, and its high-dimensional form drives concentration. We connect the boundary-mass and equator-mass phenomena to a single isoperimetric principle, then preview how these volume facts feed later chapters on embeddings and approximation.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: We close by gathering the chapter's through-line: the ball volume formula, the rise-then-collapse, boundary and equator concentration, ellipsoid approximation, covering numbers, and volume hardness. Each is a facet of the same high-dimensional intuition, and together they prepare the reader for the algorithmic geometry that follows.
